USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue targeted non-tariff escalation — maintain Huawei Entity List restrictions and signal willingness to extend tariffs to remaining ~$325B of Chinese imports, but hold off on actually implementing the broad tariff expansion until after the G20 meeting with Xi later this month. The Huawei action is the most potent lever we have and should be sustained; it directly threatens China's 5G and tech-self-sufficiency agenda in ways tariff revenue never could. Use the threat of the $325B tariff round as a negotiating stick, not a fait accompli — deploying it prematurely would raise consumer prices on everyday goods and invite broader retaliation before we've tested whether the current pressure is enough to extract meaningful concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US holds a clear structural advantage in this dispute as of early June 2019. The tariff asymmetry is stark: we have $250B of Chinese goods under 25% tariffs with $325B more available, while China has retaliated on only $60B of US goods and has limited room to escalate further given the trade imbalance ($540B vs $125B in bilateral imports). China's economy is showing visible stress — April industrial production collapsed to 5.4% growth (from 8.5% in March), retail sales hit a 16-year low at 7.2%, and the manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in May. The Huawei Entity List action, implemented May 16, strikes directly at China's most vulnerable point: its dependence on US semiconductor technology for 5G infrastructure and smartphone production. Qualcomm, Intel, and other US suppliers are hurt in the short term (shares fell 3-7% on announcement), but the leverage this creates over China's tech ambitions is asymmetric — Huawei itself admitted it needs US components for 5G base stations. China's counter-threats are manageable: the rare earth gambit is 'loud saber-rattling' per analysts, since the US accounts for only 9% of global rare earth demand ($160M in imports) and alternatives exist in Malaysia and Australia. China's 'unreliable entity list' (announced May 31) is retaliatory signaling but lacks the precision of US export controls. The domestic US economy remains fundamentally strong — Q1 GDP was 3.2%, unemployment is low — though the S&P 500's 6.6% May decline and rising production costs (59% of ISM firms affected) signal that indefinite escalation carries real costs. The OECD estimates full escalation could shave 0.8% off US GDP. The G20 later this month offers a natural test point: if Xi signals willingness to negotiate on structural issues (IP protection, forced tech transfer, enforcement mechanisms), the US can moderate. If not, the $325B tariff threat remains available. Key risk is overplaying: implementing the full $325B would directly hit US consumer goods (electronics, clothing, toys) and could shift domestic political sentiment against the trade war ahead of the 2020 election cycle.

Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi (widely read as a signal on rare-earth leverage).
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
China announces it will establish an 'unreliable entity list' targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.

China's rare earths threat is no game changer — U.S. accounted for only 9% of global demand for rare earths, spending only $160 million in 2018 to import them.
OECD said full escalation scenario could knock 0.8% off US GDP and 1.1% off Chinese GDP by 2021-22.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Retaliate asymmetrically against the US Huawei escalation by deploying the unreliable entity list against US firms cutting supply to Chinese companies, and signal readiness to restrict rare earth exports. Do not initiate new tariff escalation, but do not concede anything while under maximum pressure. Maintain the posture that the door to negotiation remains open, but only from a position of demonstrated counter-leverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is HIGH and escalating rapidly. Three factors drive the +0.65 threat score:

(a) The Huawei Entity List action (May 16) is qualitatively different from tariff escalation — it targets China's core technology ambitions. Huawei is the world's largest telecom equipment maker and second-largest smartphone seller; cutting off US chip and Android supply chains directly threatens Made in China 2025 goals. Export orders sub-index plunged to 46.5 from 49.2 (NBS May PMI), the sharpest deterioration in the survey.

(b) The manufacturing economy is already contracting: PMI fell to 49.4 in May (below the 50 expansion threshold, worse than analyst expectations of 49.9). Employment hit 47.0, the lowest since March 2009. Industrial profits fell 3.7% in April — the steepest decline in 3.5 years. Retail sales growth hit a 16-year low at 7.2%. The $200B List 3 tariff hike from 10% to 25% (effective May 10) is compounding the damage, and a further ~$300B in tariffs is being prepared, which would cover virtually all Chinese exports to the US.

(c) This is no longer a trade dispute — it has become a technology war with national security framing (EO 13873 on ICT supply chains). The Fitch estimate of 0.5% GDP drag from the escalation would push China to the lower bound of its 6.0-6.5% growth target, risking unemployment in export hubs and potential social instability.

The action_score of -0.55 (moderate escalation, retaliatory framing) is justified because: (1) China's rare earth leverage is real — China controls ~90% of global supply, critical for semiconductors, electronics, and military equipment. Xi's May 20 visit to a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi was a deliberate signal, and the NDRC's subsequent veiled threats have prepared the domestic and international audience. (2) The unreliable entity list (announced May 31) provides a legal framework to counter-target US firms like Google and chip suppliers who severed Huawei ties under US government pressure. (3) Concession under maximum pressure would signal weakness and invite further demands on structural issues (IP, state subsidies, SOEs) that Beijing cannot accept without undermining CCP economic governance. (4) However, the escalation must be measured — broad tariff retaliation beyond the existing $60B list would further damage China's own export economy when PMI is already contracting. Asymmetric retaliation (rare earths, entity list) preserves leverage while limiting self-harm.
